1114.title: Raga Basant
1114.hook: the raga of spring, and a line about a month when it is always spring
1114.howItsDone: In kirtan, shabads from the Basant section of the Guru Granth Sahib are sung in Raga Basant, and tradition gives the raga a special place in the spring season.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a hymn in Bhairao, and your line was the milk offering: Namdev's cup, offered to someone present. A new week starts now.

Somewhere in the Guru Granth Sahib there's a line that does something strange to the calendar. It praises a month, then says that in this month spring is always present. Always. Not for a few weeks between the cold and the heat. A spring that doesn't end. It opens today's raga, Basant, the raga of spring, which tradition sings when the actual spring comes round. So there are two springs in this section. One arrives with the season. The other, the Granth suggests, is something else entirely.
screen: `A MONTH WHEN SPRING IS ALWAYS PRESENT.` → `TWO SPRINGS.` → `RAGA BASANT.`

segments.voice: Basant comes right after Bhairao in the Granth's order. It's also an ordinary word for spring, and the raga carries the season in its name. Tradition sings it in springtime, so here a raga is not only a mood but a calendar: you'd hear these hymns as the fields turn green. The opening hymn, by Guru Nanak, in paraphrase: of all the months, blessed is the month in which spring is always present. Blossom, my mind, by remembering the One. That's the first move. The Guru takes the season everyone waits for, makes it permanent, and hands it to the mind. The second move comes in a hymn by Guru Amar Das further in. In paraphrase: spring has come, and all the green growth has flowered. And these living beings flower too, when they fix their attention on God. Notice the two levels side by side. Outside, a real spring with real blossoms; the hymns don't pretend it isn't lovely. Inside, a flowering that needs no date on the calendar, because it comes from where the mind rests. A field blooms once a year. The Granth's spring is always present, because the One it remembers is always present. So when the season comes round and the gurdwara sings Basant, the outer spring becomes a reminder of the inner one. Today's line is simple: spring.
screen: `BASANT: THE SEASON IN THE NAME.` · `A MONTH WHEN SPRING IS ALWAYS PRESENT.` · `BLOSSOM, MY MIND.` · `THE FIELD BLOOMS; SO DO THE BEINGS.` · then, large: `SPRING.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind, or look at, one living thing near you, a plant on the sill, a tree outside, even a weed in a crack of the pavement, and notice that it's growing right now, too slowly to see. Breathe slowly with it, then turn the same attention inward, gently, without forcing anything to bloom. If you pray, remember the One the way Guru Nanak's line asks, blossom, my mind; if you don't, simply rest with the green thing.
Raga Basant. The raga of spring, which follows Bhairao, sung by tradition in the spring season, and opening with Guru Nanak's month in which spring is always present. Today's word.
Your line: spring. In Basant, the inner spring doesn't wait for the season. See you tomorrow.

1115.title: A hymn in Basant
1115.hook: Ramanand sets out for the temple with sandalwood, and is turned back toward his own heart
1115.howItsDone: Ramanand's hymn is sung in kirtan in Raga Basant, alongside the Gurus' own hymns; Sikhs honor the Bhagats whose words the Gurus placed in the Guru Granth Sahib.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Raga Basant, and your line was spring: a month in which spring is always present.

Sandalwood, ground into a paste on a stone. Fragrant oils in small bottles. A man gathers them up, the way you'd gather what you need for something important, and sets out to worship God in a temple. He has everything ready. And somewhere between his door and the temple, his plan changes. The man is the Bhagat Ramanand, and he tells the story himself, in a hymn the Gurus placed in the Basant section of the Guru Granth Sahib.
screen: `SANDALWOOD AND FRAGRANT OILS.` → `HE SETS OUT FOR THE TEMPLE.` → `THE PLAN CHANGES.`

segments.voice: The hymn begins at the end of the story, with a question. In paraphrase: where should I go? My own home has been colored with joy. My mind no longer wanders; it has gone still. Then he tells us how. One day a longing rose in him. He ground sandalwood with fragrant oils and set out to worship God in the temple. But that God, he says, the Guru showed him inside his own heart. Wherever he went after that, he found the One already there, present in everything. The hymn ends with thanks: he offers himself to the true Guru, who cut away his confusion and doubt, and names his Lord as the One who pervades all. Tradition remembers Ramanand as a teacher other Bhagats looked to, and links Kabir with him; the hymn itself says nothing about that, so hold it as tradition. What the hymn does say is the turn from going to staying. The sandalwood isn't mocked. The longing that sent him out the door is real, and the hymn honors it as the start of the story. But the finding happens at home. And the word for what happens to his home is rang, the same word used for dye and for love. His house is dyed with it. Yesterday the Granth spoke of a spring always present. Today Ramanand shows where it was all along: not out on the road, but in the house, in the heart. Your line: spring at home.
screen: `WHERE SHOULD I GO?` · `MY HOME IS COLORED WITH JOY.` · `SHOWN GOD IN HIS OWN HEART.` · `THE FINDING HAPPENS AT HOME.` · then, large: `SPRING AT HOME.`

segments.voice: If you can, play a shabad sung in Basant, or sit in the quiet, and notice the room around you exactly as it is: the light, the sounds, the slightly untidy corner, resisting the small urge to be somewhere better. Then bring your attention to the breath and rest there, as if you've just come home after a long trip. If you pray, remember the One the hymn says is already present; if you don't, simply let this room be enough for now.
A hymn in Basant. Ramanand's song of setting out with sandalwood to worship, and being shown God in his own heart, so that his home is colored with joy. Today's word.
Your line: spring at home. Ramanand's longing set him on the road, and the finding happened at home. Until tomorrow.

1116.title: Raga Sarang
1116.hook: a raga for the hot middle of the day, and a Guru who calls himself a servant
1116.howItsDone: In kirtan, shabads from the Sarang section of the Guru Granth Sahib are sung in Raga Sarang, which tradition associates with the midday hours, and the Var of Sarang is sung or read in the sangat.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ramanand's hymn in Basant, and your line was spring at home: shown God in his own heart.

Noon on a hot street. The shadow of a lamppost has shrunk to a dark puddle at its foot. Phones buzz, inboxes fill, and the day is at its loudest, half gone and half still to do. The Guru Granth Sahib has a raga that tradition gives to this hot, bright middle. It's called Sarang. So what does its first hymn do with the busiest part of the day?
screen: `NOON ON A HOT STREET.` → `THE DAY AT ITS LOUDEST.` → `RAGA SARANG.`

segments.voice: Sarang follows Basant in the Granth's order, so the book moves from spring to the heat of the day. Tradition sings it in the midday hours, and later in the section there's also a Var, a ballad of stanzas with saloks between them, by Guru Ram Das. The section opens with a hymn of Guru Nanak, and its first line is a surprise from a Guru. In paraphrase: I am the servant girl of my own Master. I have taken hold of the feet of God, the life of the world, and my ego has been settled and put to rest. In the Granth the Gurus sometimes speak in the voice of a bride or a servant before God, and here the picture is of someone who has stopped running the house and simply holds on to the Master. Now set that at noon. Midday is when the self is busiest: deciding, answering, pushing the list along. It's the easiest hour to feel in charge of everything. The opening of Sarang puts a different picture at its center: not someone on top of the day, but someone holding the feet of the One who gives the world its life, with the ego quiet. That doesn't mean stopping work. In the hymn's picture the work goes on, but the house has a Master, and it isn't the servant. A shadow at noon is small, because the sun is right overhead. The hymn's ego is small for the same reason. Today's line: midday.
screen: `AFTER BASANT: THE HEAT OF THE DAY.` · `I AM THE SERVANT OF MY OWN MASTER.` · `HOLDING THE FEET, EGO AT REST.` · `A SMALL SHADOW AT NOON.` · then, large: `MIDDAY.`

segments.voice: Wherever you are in the day, stop what you're running for a minute: put your hands down, palms open, as if you've set down the keys to the whole operation, and if it's near noon, let a shabad in Raga Sarang play. Breathe slowly, notice how much of you was busy being in charge, and let some of it rest. If you pray, hold Guru Nanak's picture of holding the Master's feet; if you don't, simply let the open hands do the work.
Raga Sarang. The midday raga after Basant, opening with Guru Nanak as the servant of his own Master, his ego at rest. Today's word.
Your line: midday. In Sarang's first hymn, the work goes on, but the house has a Master. Back tomorrow, same hill.

1117.title: A hymn in Sarang
1117.hook: Parmanand asks what all your listening has done, and Surdas says whose company to leave
1117.howItsDone: The Bhagats' hymns in Raga Sarang, Parmanand's among them, are sung in kirtan beside the Gurus' own, and Sikhs join hearing the Word with seva such as serving food in the langar.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Raga Sarang, and your line was midday: Guru Nanak as the servant of his own Master.

What have you done, by listening? That's roughly the question that opens today's hymn, and it's a sharp one in a series where every day has asked you to listen. A person sits through the holy stories, hears them told and retold, nods along. Then the hymn asks: and what came of it? It's by the Bhagat Parmanand, one of the voices the Gurus set inside the Sarang section of the Guru Granth Sahib. Near it stands a short verse under the name of Surdas.
screen: `WHAT HAVE YOU DONE, BY LISTENING?` → `PARMANAND ASKS.` → `SURDAS STANDS NEARBY.`

segments.voice: Here's Parmanand's hymn, in paraphrase. O man, what have you gained from hearing the Puranas told? Steady devotion hasn't welled up in you, and you haven't given to the hungry. Lust hasn't left you, and neither has anger. Greed hasn't let go. You haven't stopped slandering others. Then, in its closing line, the hymn names the company of the holy. Notice the target. Not the stories; Parmanand doesn't say a word against them. It's the listener who hears and stays the same. In the hymn, hearing is supposed to go somewhere: into devotion that holds steady, and into food on a hungry person's plate. If it goes nowhere, the hymn asks what it was for. Surdas's verse makes a matching point from the other side. In paraphrase: O mind, leave the company of those who have turned their backs on the Lord. Parmanand says hearing alone won't change you. Surdas says the people around you will, one way or the other. Together they picture a devotion that isn't only an ear. It's hands and feet and the people you sit with. Now set it in Sarang, the midday raga. Midday is lunchtime, the hour when someone who has listened all morning finds out whether any of it reached their hands: whether someone hungry gets fed, whether the slander at the lunch table gets joined or left. That's the line for today: midday devotion.
screen: `WHAT HAVE YOU GAINED FROM HEARING?` · `NO DEVOTION, NO FOOD FOR THE HUNGRY.` · `SURDAS: LEAVE THAT COMPANY.` · `LISTENING THAT REACHES THE HANDS.` · then, large: `MIDDAY DEVOTION.`

segments.voice: If you can, play a shabad sung in Sarang, or sit in the quiet, and ask yourself Parmanand's question without judging: of all the good things I've heard lately, what has reached my hands? Let one answer come, even a small one, then one thing your hands could do today, a meal shared, a kind word in place of a sharp one, and just hold it. If you pray, say Waheguru on each slow breath; if you don't, simply breathe.
A hymn in Sarang. Parmanand's question to the person who hears the holy stories and doesn't change, with Surdas's verse beside it about the company you keep. Today's word.
Your line: midday devotion. In Parmanand's hymn, listening is meant to reach the hands. See you tomorrow.

1118.title: Raga Malar
1118.hook: the monsoon raga opens not with rain but with what everyone forgets
1118.howItsDone: In kirtan, shabads from the Malar section of the Guru Granth Sahib are sung in Raga Malar, which tradition associates with the monsoon and sings in the rainy season.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Parmanand's hymn in Sarang, and your line was midday devotion: listening that reaches the hands.

The first fat drops hit the dry street, and the smell changes before anything else does. Then the sky opens. People who were walking start running. Someone pulls laundry off a line. A child stands in the yard with her face up and her mouth open. For a few minutes, everyone stops and looks up. Rain does that. The Guru Granth Sahib has a raga that tradition gives to the rainy season, called Malar. And its first hymn makes everyone look up, without a drop of rain in it.
screen: `THE FIRST DROPS ON A DRY STREET.` → `EVERYONE STOPS AND LOOKS UP.` → `RAGA MALAR.`

segments.voice: Malar follows Sarang in the Granth's order, so the book moves from the heat of midday to the rains that break it. Tradition calls Malar the monsoon raga and sings it in the rainy season. Its pages are full of rain pictures: clouds, thunder, the bird that cries out for a single drop. But here's the surprise. The section opens with a hymn of Guru Nanak that isn't about rain at all. In paraphrase: eating, drinking, laughing, sleeping, we have forgotten dying. Forgetting the Master, we've brought ourselves to ruin; a life like that won't last. Then the turn: meditate on the one Name, and go home with your honor. A hard first line for a rain song? Think back to the street. Eating, drinking, laughing, sleeping: that's the ordinary loop, and it's fine, until it runs so smoothly that a person forgets where it ends. Then the rain comes, the loop breaks for a few minutes, and everyone looks up. Malar's opening does the same thing in words. It interrupts, just long enough to ask what the routine has made you forget. And rain in a hot country isn't gloomy. It's relief, what lets the fields live. Guru Nanak's interruption comes the same way: a hard word about a life that won't last, and then relief, the one Name, and the way home with honor. Today's line: rain.
screen: `AFTER SARANG: THE RAINS BREAK THE HEAT.` · `EATING, DRINKING, LAUGHING, SLEEPING.` · `WE HAVE FORGOTTEN DYING.` · `RAIN INTERRUPTS, AND GIVES LIFE.` · then, large: `RAIN.`

segments.voice: If it's raining, open a window a little and listen, or play a shabad sung in Malar; if not, sit in the quiet and let this minute be the interruption: no eating, no scrolling, no planning, just slow breath. Look up, at the ceiling or the sky, and let one honest thought come about where your days are going, without arguing with it. If you pray, hold Guru Nanak's line about the one Name; if you don't, simply look up.
Raga Malar. The monsoon raga that follows Sarang, sung by tradition in the rains, opening with Guru Nanak's line that in eating, drinking, laughing and sleeping we have forgotten dying. Today's word.
Your line: rain. In Malar, the hard word comes first, and then the relief, like rain. Until tomorrow.

1119.title: A hymn in Malar
1119.hook: a plea to the clouds not to wait, and Ravidas naming his family's work out loud
1119.howItsDone: Hymns from the Malar section, the Gurus' and the Bhagats', Ravidas's among them, are sung in kirtan in Raga Malar, and tradition sings them in the rainy season.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Raga Malar, and your line was rain: an interruption that brings relief.

Rain, dear cloud. Don't wait even a moment. That's a line from a hymn of Guru Arjan in Malar, in plain English, spoken the way a farmer might speak to a sky that has been holding back. Rain, beloved, and hold up my mind. A few pages on, in the same raga, a very different voice speaks to the people of his town about his own family and the work they do. Two songs, and what the rain has to do with both.
screen: `RAIN, DEAR CLOUD.` → `DON'T WAIT EVEN A MOMENT.` → `A DIFFERENT VOICE, SAME RAGA.`

segments.voice: First, the rain. In Guru Arjan's hymn, in paraphrase: rain, dear cloud, don't delay. Rain, beloved, hold up my mind, and let joy and longing fill it. The cloud stands for God's grace, and the dry field is the mind waiting for it. And the rain doesn't choose which field to fall on. Now the second voice, one you met on day 774: Ravidas, whose hymns stand near the end of Malar. He speaks to the townspeople and names his caste out loud: a leather worker, known to everyone. In my heart, he says, I hold the praises of the Lord. In another hymn he goes further. In paraphrase: my family still goes around Benares carrying away dead cattle. And yet now the learned Brahmins of the city bow before their son, Ravidas, the servant of servants, because he has taken refuge in your Name. In Kedara, at dusk, Ravidas let the labels fade. Here he says his out loud, in public, and doesn't apologize. He states the work plainly, work others looked down on, then says what changed: not his birth, not his family's trade, but the Name. The Gurus placed his words in the Granth, to be sung and bowed to beside their own. The rain falls on every field alike. The Name, in Ravidas's hymn, falls on a leather worker's son exactly as on anyone. So a rain song isn't only about weather. It's about grace that doesn't check your family name first. Your line: the rain song.

segments.voice: If you can, play a shabad sung in Malar, or sit in the quiet, and bring to mind someone whose work is easy to overlook: the person who collects your trash, cleans the building, cares for the sick through the night. 1120.title: Raga Kanara
1120.hook: a night raga that opens with a mind turned green by good company
1120.howItsDone: In kirtan, shabads from the Kanara section of the Guru Granth Sahib are sung in Raga Kanara, which tradition associates with the night, and the Var of Kanara is sung or read in the sangat.

segments.voice: Yesterday, two songs in Malar, and your line was the rain song: grace falling on every field alike.

The dinner ended hours ago, but nobody has left the table. The plates are pushed aside, the candle has burned low, and the talk has gone past small things into real ones. When the guests finally go, the house is dark and quiet, and somehow the whole place feels lighter than it did at sunset. Good company can do that. The Guru Granth Sahib has a raga tradition sings late, after dark, called Kanara, and its very first hymn is about exactly that kind of company.
screen: `NOBODY HAS LEFT THE TABLE.` → `LIGHTER THAN AT SUNSET.` → `RAGA KANARA.`

segments.voice: Kanara follows Malar in the Granth's order, so after the rains comes the night. Tradition gives it to the late hours. Its pages hold hymns of Guru Ram Das and Guru Arjan, and a Var, a ballad with saloks between its stanzas, by Guru Ram Das. It opens with a hymn of Guru Ram Das. In paraphrase: my mind has turned green, meeting the holy people. I am a sacrifice to them. Meeting them, I am carried across. Green. A mind that turns green has come back to life, the way a dry field greens after rain. And notice where the greening comes from: not from being alone with a great thought, but from meeting people, the sadh sangat, the company of the holy. You met the sangat way back on day 15. Now set it at night. The day's company is gone, and what remains is whatever it left in you. Kanara opens by saying good company leaves something green. And at the end of a week, look how far the ragas have walked. Basant's spring always present, and Ramanand's spring at home. Sarang's midday heat, with Guru Nanak as a servant and Parmanand's hard question at lunchtime. Malar's rain breaking the heat, and Ravidas's rain song falling on every field. Now night, and a mind turning green again. Spring to night, green to green. Your line for today is the hour itself: night.
screen: `AFTER THE RAINS, THE NIGHT.` · `MY MIND HAS TURNED GREEN.` · `MEETING THE HOLY PEOPLE.` · `THE WEEK: SPRING, MIDDAY, RAIN, NIGHT.` · then, large: `NIGHT.`

segments.voice: If it's evening, dim the lights and let a shabad in Raga Kanara play, or sit in the quiet, and bring to mind one person whose company left you lighter this week. Don't analyze it; let their face be there for a few slow breaths, and notice whatever is green in you because of them. If you pray, remember Guru Ram Das's thanks for the holy company; if you don't, a quiet thank-you in your own mind is enough.
Raga Kanara. The night raga that follows Malar, opening with Guru Ram Das's hymn of a mind turned green by meeting the holy people. Today's word.
